query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Lightweight high-entropy alloys can combine low density with high mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance when their inherently stabilized, multi-principal element microstructure facilitates the in-situ formation of a uniform nano-scale oxide film and concomitant grain refinement. This oxide layer acts as a dual mediator by impeding oxygen and corrosive species diffusion while promoting grain-boundary strengthening that enhances both strength and resistance to environmental degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a high-entropy stabilized matrix and initially moderate grain size, lacking a purposely induced oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal oxidation treatment under defined oxygen partial pressures combined with mechanical processing (e.g., deformation) to induce dynamic grain refinement.
generation.conditions: Exposure to environments with controlled oxygen availability at high temperatures (600–800 °C) and subsequent testing in corrosive (e.g., saline) media; room temperature and elevated temperature mechanical load tests.
generation.structural_mediator: A nano-scale, adherent oxide film distributed both at the surface and along grain boundaries, accompanied by a refined grain structure.
generation.mechanism: The alloy’s multi-element composition encourages slowed diffusion and a stabilized high-entropy state that promotes the formation of a protective oxide film during thermal treatment. This film serves as a diffusion barrier, significantly reducing oxygen and corrosive species ingress. Simultaneously, mechanical processing leads to grain refinement which imparts enhanced strength through grain-boundary strengthening effects, possibly invoking an inverse Hall-Petch behavior in the nano-scale regime.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline alloys processed without controlled oxidation or grain refinement, the treated lightweight high-entropy alloys should exhibit increased yield strength, lower corrosion current densities, and improved high-temperature oxidation resistance due to the presence of the uniform oxide layer and refined microstructure.
generation.baseline: A control lightweight high-entropy alloy that is processed conventionally without specialized thermal oxidation or post-deformation grain refinement treatments.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to fail if the alloy composition deviates significantly from a high-entropy design (leading to phase segregation) or if the processing conditions (e.g., excessively aggressive or high-temperature environments) destabilize the protective oxide film, thereby negating its barrier functionality.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal oxide film thickness and its precise composition, as well as the quantitative relationship between grain refinement and strength enhancements, remain to be rigorously determined. Moreover, the sensitivity of the mechanism to minor compositional variations is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of lightweight high-entropy alloy samples with identical base compositions. Process one set with controlled thermal oxidation and mechanical deformation treatments to induce the formation of a protective oxide film and refined microstructure. Process the other set via conventional methods without specialized treatments. Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation tests, corrosion tests in saline environments, and mechanical strength tests at room and elevated temperatures.
measurements: Oxide film thickness and uniformity (using TEM/SEM analysis)
Grain size distribution (using electron backscatter diffraction or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the selectively treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in yield strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance compared to the control group or if the predicted nano-scale oxide film with refined grains is not observed, then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

A strong and ductile medium-entropy alloy resists hydrogen embrittlement and corrosion

Abstract: AbstractStrong and ductile materials that have high resistance to corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement are rare and yet essential for realizing safety-critical energy infrastructures, hydrogen-based industries, and transportation solutions. Here we report how we reconcile these constraints in the form of a strong and ductile CoNiV medium-entropy alloy with face-centered cubic structure. It shows high resistance to hydrogen embrittlement at ambient temperature at a strain rate of 10−4 s−1, due to its low hydrogen diffusivity and the deformation twinning that impedes crack propagation. Moreover, a dense oxide film formed on the alloy’s surface reduces the hydrogen uptake rate, and provides high corrosion resistance in dilute sulfuric acid with a corrosion current density below 7 μA cm−2. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 High-Entropy Alloy for Corrosion Resistance Coatings

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
